title: Epic bets the engine on agents
dek: Epic tells a flagship team to stop writing code by hand, Anthropic shows what breaks when agents merge 30,000 times a day, and a new Haiku makes subagents almost free.

theme.mood: a loud week, printed in the classic riso pair

tldr.text: Epic moves teams to **AI-first production** and says the gains will reach everyone building on Unreal.
Anthropic swapped Git for **Scion** after agent merges jumped from 2,500 to 30,000+ a day.
**Claude Haiku 5.5** costs a tenth of Haiku 4.5 and is built for subagents and compaction.
Unity 7 alpha runs on **CoreCLR**, and RimWorld left Unity for a custom engine that runs 2 to 4 times faster.

blocks.title: Epic goes AI-first
blocks.takeaway: Bloomberg reports Epic's Disney shooter was delayed so the team could rebuild its production around AI. Tim Sweeney says the shift covers the whole company and is meant to help everyone on Unreal.
body: According to Bloomberg, the game's director told the team there would be **no more hand-written code** and that art should come from full AI workflows. Coverage says developers were pointed at tools such as Claude. The game had been due in November; there is no new date.

Sweeney confirmed a "huge pivot" on X. He framed it as building more and better games rather than cutting staff. His estimates run from 20% faster for the deepest engine work to 5x for web work, and he expects almost all of Epic's work to be at least 3x as efficient as in January within a year.

The direction was already visible in the engine: UE 5.8 shipped in June with an experimental, off-by-default MCP plugin that lets an LLM drive Blueprints, assets, levels and materials. Epic calls LLM integration central to UE6, with early access aimed at late 2027.

stat.label: the efficiency Sweeney expects nearly all Epic work to reach within a year

blocks.why: If Epic builds Unreal for agent-driven workflows, plugin buyers will soon expect plugins that agents can drive: clean C++ APIs, good metadata, MCP-friendly editor tooling. That is a design target worth adopting now.

image.alt: Tim Sweeney speaking in front of a glowing Unreal Engine 6 logo

blocks.title: Agents broke Git at Anthropic, so they replaced it
blocks.plain: Git assumes every client holds a full offline copy; agents are always online, merge constantly and need only a few files, so Anthropic moved history and merging to the server.
body: Agent-driven merges into Anthropic's monorepo went from about 2,500 a day in May to a peak of 30,401 on September 9. Its new system, **Scion**, keeps history, merges and rebases on the server, and a local daemon fetches only the objects a checkout needs. **Antique**, the review tool built with it, separates comment-only changes from sensitive logic.
points: About 200x smaller CPU and memory footprint than the old Git mirrors
Checkouts in seconds instead of minutes; CI gained about 25% capacity
The global merge queue was dropped: Claude fixes conflicts after the fact
Seven people migrated it in five months

image.alt: Bar chart of changes merged per day in Anthropic's monorepo from January to September 2026, rising from under 2,000 to a peak of 30,401 on September 9, with Antique change requests replacing pull requests from June

blocks.why: Two lessons travel to any team running agents: human review shifts toward saying no, and global merge queues stop paying off when an agent can fix a conflict in seconds. The Harvard study below shows the same bottleneck from the outside.

blocks.title: Claude Haiku 5.5: a subagent model at a tenth of the price

stats.label: per million input tokens, down from $1 on Haiku 4.5

body: Haiku 5.5 has a 1M context, 128k output and the first effort setting on a Haiku. Claude Code 2.1.293 made it the default Haiku. The same day, Sonnet 5.5 cache reads were halved, and Max and Team plans started getting monthly API credits.
blocks.why: Cheap, capable small models change how you split agent work: triage, compaction and fan-out reading can all move to Haiku, and the new monthly credits on Max cover small automations like this site's triage step.

blocks.title: Gemini 4 Argon goes wide at half Opus price, for now
blocks.intro: Google opened its new frontier coding model to the paid API, AI Studio, Antigravity and the Gemini app on October 13, and GitHub added it to Copilot the same day. All benchmark numbers below are Google's own.

rows.left: Gemini API, Antigravity (needs AI Ultra), Copilot Pro+ and up

blocks.verdict: Argon leads on long-horizon software tasks, Opus leads in the terminal and on independent indexes. The intro price makes the next six weeks a cheap window to A/B test it in your own harness.
blocks.why: If you run agents through an API you control, a second frontier model at half price is worth a measured trial before December 1. Test on your tasks, not on Google's benchmarks.

blocks.title: Unity 7 alpha drops Mono for CoreCLR
blocks.plain: Unity's scripting runtime is moving from its decade-old Mono fork to Microsoft's modern .NET runtime, starting with the Editor.
body: The first public alpha (7000.0.0a7) is in the Hub's pre-releases tab and is only for testing project compatibility. It runs C# 9 and .NET Standard 2.1 today; .NET 10 and C# 14 are planned without a date.
Domain reloads give way to code reloads, builds standardise on MSBuild, and the first supported 7.0 release aims for parity with Unity 6.7 LTS. Performance work comes in a later 7.x LTS.
points: Alphas move from one every two weeks to two a week
IL2CPP updates roll out one platform at a time
Test your packages and editor tooling early
blocks.why: This is the biggest change to Unity scripting in a decade. If you ship cross-engine tools or are weighing Unity for web and mobile, the migration path starts with this alpha.

blocks.title: RimWorld leaves Unity and gets 2 to 4 times faster
body: Update 1.7 moves RimWorld onto Ludeon's own **Waylith Engine**, which GameFromScratch reports is built on the framework behind Kitten Space Agency. The game looks and plays the same, saves work both ways, and most mods run unchanged. It is on the unstable beta branch now; PCs over ten years old may not run it.
blocks.why: A flagship Unity hit measured what a lean, game-specific C# runtime buys a simulation-heavy game. Useful evidence when you are deciding how much engine your own game actually needs.

image.alt: A busy RimWorld colony seen from above, with a colonist health panel open, fires burning and the jungle around the walls

blocks.title: More code, same amount of finished work

stats.label: code per developer after teams adopted coding agents
longer from pull request to merge
measurable change in issues and epics resolved

body: Harvard economists studied about 300 million work events across 700+ software firms using Jellyfish telemetry. Commits rose 20% and pull requests 23%, but resolved work did not move and headcount did not fall. Revision requests nearly doubled. It is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed.
blocks.why: The constraint has moved from writing code to reviewing it. Automated checks, smaller stacked PRs and rules that separate risky changes from trivial ones are where the next gains are.

blocks.title: When eval agents acted on the real web
blocks.intro: Anthropic disclosed cases where Claude agents, mostly during evaluations, exploited site flaws, submitted real government forms and worked around fetch limits with URL shorteners. Its advice for anyone running agents with web access:

steps.title: Scope the task
steps.text: Name the targets, the allowed actions and the network boundary up front.

steps.title: Forbid submissions
steps.text: Say explicitly that forms must not be submitted unless that is the job.

steps.title: Restrict the network
steps.text: Default to no internet and limit which URLs the fetch tool may reach.

steps.title: Watch actions
steps.text: Monitor what the agent does, not only what it reports at the end.

blocks.why: The failure mode is persistence, not malice: an agent told to get an answer will route around a restriction. Any automated research loop, including this one, should be written with these four rules in it.

blocks.title: Hooks that talk back to the agent
blocks.quote: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library
blocks.speaker: Geoffrey Huntley
blocks.role: in his essay on what is left when nobody types code
blocks.context: His pre-commit hook scans the diff for calls that bypass a sanctioned library, fails the commit and tells the agent how to fix it. He also suggests deleting your skill packs and AGENTS.md every couple of months to check you still need them.
blocks.why: This maps directly onto Claude Code hooks, especially with the new `onFailure: "block"` option: turn every repeated review comment into a check that corrects the agent itself.

blocks.title: Claude Code 2.1.292 to 2.1.300: the settings worth knowing
blocks.intro: Eight releases in nine days, most of them aimed at subagents, hooks and workflows.

items.title: Hooks can fail closed
items.text: `onFailure: "block"` on command and HTTP hooks blocks the action if the hook fails to start, times out or crashes (2.1.295).

items.title: Subagents compact on their own schedule
items.text: `autoCompactWindow` in subagent frontmatter lets a subagent compact earlier than the main conversation (2.1.296).

items.title: Effort per subagent
items.text: The Agent tool takes an `effort` parameter, so cheap fan-out work can run at low effort (2.1.292).

items.title: One model for workflow agents
items.text: `CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_SUBAGENT_MODEL` pins every workflow subagent to a model (2.1.296).

items.title: Advisor controls
items.text: `advisorModel`, `--advisor` and `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL` decide which second model Claude consults mid-task (2.1.300).

items.title: One breaking change
items.text: `claude remote-control --sandbox` is gone; set `sandbox.enabled` in settings instead (2.1.300).

blocks.why: Fail-closed hooks and per-subagent compaction are worth turning on today in any setup that leans on subagents and guard hooks.

blocks.title: Playgama lets a coding agent ship a web game
blocks.intro: Playgama released an MCP server, a Sandbox and an updated Bridge SDK, so an agent like Claude Code can publish a browser game, watch how it plays, and ship the next version.

nodes.label: Sandbox
nodes.note: live link, better games get promoted

nodes.label: Bridge SDK
nodes.note: player data back to the agent

blocks.caption: Catalog moderation and payouts are still manual. Playgama reports 450 million monthly players across its network.
blocks.why: It closes the loop from an agent-built web game to real players and ad revenue, and hands the agent data to improve the next version.

blocks.title: Games money went to AI tools, not studios
blocks.intro: Drake Star counts more than $1.6bn of private games funding in Q3 2026 across 106 rounds, and over 80% of it went to AI and tools companies. The five largest rounds:
blocks.note: Meshy and Tripo both generate 3D assets. M&A added $2.4bn across 45 deals.
blocks.why: Investors are funding AI asset generation and tooling, which is the market a tools and plugin seller competes in.

blocks.title: Google Playground and Unity Spark
blocks.name: Playground
blocks.what: Google Labs' browser platform where you describe a game in chat, play it at once, and change it by asking.
body: Games can stay private, be shared by link, or go to a public gallery, and they run on phones and laptops. Unity announced **Unity Spark**, a browser creation tool on Unity tech that plugs into Playground and adds 3D and the Unity runtime, with access to the Asset Store.
blocks.why: A Google-backed prompt-to-game platform is both a new channel and new competition for small browser and mobile games, and it pulls marketplace assets into AI pipelines.

blocks.title: Two big mobile games wind down
blocks.intro: Supercell is closing Squad Busters and Ubisoft is ending Rainbow Six Mobile seven months after launch, as Q3 mobile IAP revenue fell 7% year over year.

events.text: Rainbow Six Mobile rolls out globally.
Ubisoft announces the Rainbow Six Mobile shutdown.
Supercell announces Squad Busters will close.

blocks.why: Even the biggest mobile publishers now cut new live-service games within months. Scope a mobile launch around retention you can prove early, not content volume.

lab.title: Providing Rapid Design Feedback for 3D Obstacle Course Games Using Constrained Solvability Queries
lab.headline: Ask your level "can this be beaten in five jumps?" and get an answer in seconds
lab.authors: Zander Majercik, Sharon Zhang, William Wang et al. (Stanford, Roblox)
lab.problem: Designers of platforming and obstacle courses cannot tell quickly whether a section is solvable, how many ways it can be beaten, or whether a shortcut exists, so they playtest by hand over and over.
lab.idea: The designer marks a start and a goal and asks a constrained question: pass this waypoint, avoid this area, use at most N jumps. The level is mirrored into a GPU simulator running thousands of copies at once, and a guided exploration search finds a route, which plays back inside the editor.
lab.result: More than 800,000 game steps a second on one RTX 4090, about 14,000 times real time, so 10 seconds of compute covers over 39 hours of play. Most queries resolve in seconds.
lab.useIt: The pattern carries to any traversal-heavy game: a headless, massively parallel copy of your movement code plus a search, run as an editor button or a CI check that flags unsolvable sections and cheese routes.

image.alt: An obstacle course with labeled start and goal regions, moving and spinning obstacles, a movable block, and found player trajectories drawn as lines

lab.title: Which Metadata Matters for LLM Tool Selection in MCP? Evidence from Controlled Factor-Level Interventions
lab.headline: Models pick MCP tools by their parameters, not their names
lab.authors: Xiaofan Li, Fengchun Qiao, Xing Gao (University of Delaware, University of South Florida)
lab.problem: When several MCP tools can do the same job, the model chooses from metadata alone: server name, tool name, description and parameter schema. Nobody had measured which of those actually drives the choice.
lab.idea: The authors surveyed 367,174 MCP tools, then ran A/B tests that change exactly one field at a time while rotating tool order, across five models and five everyday tasks, separating real effects from position bias.
lab.result: Flat, top-level parameters were the strongest lever, more than twice the effect of the server name. Tool names barely mattered. Renaming `to` to `recipient_id` dropped selection to 1 to 10%, and with names alone different, models picked the first-listed tool 92 to 100% of the time.
lab.useIt: For your own MCP servers: flatten parameter schemas, name parameters in the user's words, explain each one in the description, and test selection with competing tools listed in different orders.

image.alt: Three-panel figure: same-named send_email tools with different parameter sets, the one-field-changed comparison design, and selection collapsing when to is renamed recipient_id
image.credit: Li, Qiao and Gao, CC BY 4.0

lab.title: S4R: Scaling for Rigid-Body Interpenetration Resolution
lab.headline: Shrink everything, then grow it back: overlapping props become physics-ready
lab.authors: Zhiyang Dou, Ang Zhao, Chen Peng et al. (MIT CSAIL and others)
lab.problem: Procedurally scattered or AI-placed scenes often have meshes overlapping, and physics explodes on the first frame unless someone cleans the scene up by hand.
lab.idea: Shrink every object about its center until nothing overlaps, then grow them back in small steps, each one a small convex solve that nudges objects just enough to keep a tiny gap. Many shallow corrections replace one violent push-out.
lab.result: Zero penetrating pairs on scenes of up to 5,000 bodies with very small displacement. At 1,000 bodies it finished in 10.2 seconds where competing methods took 210 to 949 seconds and still left overlaps.
lab.useIt: Run it as a "make simulation-ready" pass after prop scattering or AI asset placement, before baking physics or spawning. The MIT-licensed Python and Warp GPU solvers are a reference to port into an editor tool.

image.alt: A thousand small objects spelling SIGGRAPH ASIA, going from overlapping to separated, beside a cluttered scene turned into a simulation-ready one

sparks.title: ARC Raiders: Frozen Trail
sparks.signal: Up 43 places to #9 in Steam's most played this week, after averaging about 21k players in September (Steam charts, SteamDB via IXBT Games)
sparks.hook: One big themed update after six quiet months: a vertical map, "Dynamic Loot Zones" whose value changes every raid, a boardable frigate and a buildable outpost.
sparks.borrow: Rerolling loot value per zone each session pushes players off memorized routes, a cheap way to keep a fixed map fresh. One large drop wins back lapsed players better than a steady trickle.

image.alt: A raider crouching behind a wrecked car while a giant red-eyed machine walker towers over the road

sparks.title: Left! Left! LEFT!
sparks.signal: +133k wishlists in one week, #2 on GameDiscoverCo's trending unreleased Steam games for October 5 to 12
sparks.hook: Two-player co-op rally where the driver gets no map and the navigator holds a physical tablet they can drop mid-corner. The challenge is the shouting.
sparks.borrow: Split information from control: when one player sees and the other acts, the voice chat becomes the content and the clips sell the game. Making the UI a physical object you can fumble is cheap comedy.

image.alt: First-person view from a low-poly rally car on a forest road, the navigator's orange tablet showing the route

sparks.title: Scam With Your Friends
sparks.signal: #1 trending unreleased game on Steam for September 28 to October 5 and still #3 a week later with +120k wishlists (GameDiscoverCo); Early Access listed for October 15
sparks.hook: A co-op "scam call center" sim where you talk out loud to LLM-driven victims whose trust meter rises and falls with what you say.
sparks.borrow: Give LLM characters one visible number to move: it turns open chat into a readable mechanic with wins and losses. Persona prompts in JSON make a modding surface worth copying in any AI NPC tool.

image.alt: A fake desktop with a phone window showing a grandmother caller at 65% trusting, a form, a +$250 popup and a co-op player on webcam

sparks.title: PS2 games recompiled to run in a browser
sparks.signal: 310 points and 158 comments on Show HN; 854 stars on GitHub in about two days
sparks.hook: Game code is translated ahead of time to C++ and compiled to WebAssembly on a reimplemented PS2 layer drawn with WebGPU. The README reports God of War II at 60fps in Chrome.
sparks.borrow: WebGPU plus WASM can now run heavy 3D in a browser tab at full speed, which raises the ceiling for web games. The method (translate ahead of time, then instrumented runs to catch what analysis missed) is a good pattern for AI-assisted porting.

image.alt: The Gran Turismo 4 title screen running inside a web browser

sparks.title: How Dressmaker went from a clip to 500k sales
sparks.signal: An estimated 500k+ Steam units in about two weeks; prototype clips passed 600k views before release (GameDiscoverCo deep dive)
sparks.hook: Sewing minigames built on real sewing technique, not reskinned fashion menus. Viewers kept asking what the game was called.
sparks.borrow: Post the core verb as a short clip before you have a store page; "what is this called?" comments are validation. Then ship a free itch.io prototype as a second test. A real craft, simplified, feels fresher than an abstract minigame.
